html:
Bose statistics is a way of counting particles of light, worked out in 1924 by the physicist Satyendra Nath Bose at the University of Dhaka. Particles that follow it are called bosons, after him.

Bose was trying to derive Max Planck's law of radiation, the formula for how hot bodies glow, without borrowing from older physics. He treated photons as particles that cannot be told apart from one another: swapping two of them gives no new arrangement. Counting this way gave Planck's law exactly.

A journal turned his paper down, so he sent it to Albert Einstein. Einstein saw its worth, translated it into German and had it published. He then extended the idea to atoms and predicted that at very low temperatures they would crowd into a single state. That state, a Bose Einstein condensate, was first made in a laboratory in 1995.

The British physicist Paul Dirac later named the class of particles bosons. Photons and the Higgs boson are among them. Bose belongs with C. V. Raman among the scientists of colonial India whose work changed modern physics.
sum: Bose statistics is a way of counting particles of light, worked out in 1924 by the physicist Satyendra Nath Bose at the University of Dhaka. Particles that follow it are called bosons, after him.
